summary: The iX2 is the coupe-roofed version of BMW's iX1 electric small SUV, sharing its 230kW dual-motor drivetrain and roughly 65kWh usable pack but trading a little rear headroom for a sleeker tail and a slightly bigger 525-litre boot. Australian reviewers consistently rate the powertrain, cabin quality and body control highly, but call the ride firmer than the iX1's and real-world range only middling: the 2026 update with silicon-carbide inverters lifts the WLTP claim to 476km on the standard 19-inch wheels, while independent tests of the earlier car used 17.6-19.1kWh/100km. A $7,700 price cut in March 2026 dropped it to $79,900 and deleted the front-drive eDrive20 at the same time, so the range is now a single dual-motor grade.
pros: 230kW/494Nm dual-motor all-wheel drive gets it to 100km/h in a claimed 5.6 seconds, far quicker than the rear-drive Mercedes-Benz EQA 250+ it is priced against
525-litre boot is roughly 35L larger than the iX1's despite the coupe roofline, expanding to 1400L to the roof
$7,700 cut in March 2026 brought it to $79,900 before on-roads, under both the $80,809 and $91,661 luxury car tax thresholds
Adaptive M suspension gives it composed body control, and CarExpert rates its rear seat easily more comfortable than the Mercedes-Benz EQA's
1200kg braked towing capacity with the optional bar, which several small electric SUVs cannot match
cons: Range is ordinary for an $80k EV: the 476km WLTP claim compares with roughly 415km from ADAC's 17.6kWh/100km Ecotest of the earlier car, and CarExpert measured 19.1kWh/100km in mixed driving
Firmer, busier ride than the iX1, with tyre roar on coarse-chip roads
Sloping roofline costs rear headroom, and the raised battery floor leaves taller adults sitting knees-up
Now a one-grade range — the cheaper front-drive eDrive20 was discontinued in Australia in 2026, so there is no lower entry point
Buyers of the pre-cut $87,600 car lost close to 9 per cent of list overnight, which weighs on used values
